# Anchor Phenomenon: What Is the True Cost of Storms? {#u5o-anchor}

::: {.u5o-engage-box}
## 🌀 Storms cost the US billions of dollars every year

<div style="font-size: 1.2em; font-weight: 700; text-align: center; margin: 18px 0;">
Hurricanes, winter storms and floods damage homes, shut down cities and put lives at risk. How big is this problem, and what can we do about it?
</div>

- In this unit you'll figure out **how storms cause damage**: through **strong winds**, **heavy precipitation** (rain and snow) and **flooding**.
- For each of those smaller problems, you'll look at **engineering solutions** and weigh their **benefits** and **costs**.
- At the end, you'll **design your own solution** to one part of the storm damage problem.
:::

<div class="u5o-stats" role="list" aria-label="Billion-dollar winter storms, hurricanes and floods in the US, 1980 to 2024">
<div class="u5o-stat" role="listitem" style="background:#0e7490;"><b>136</b><span>billion-dollar winter storms, hurricanes and floods (1980–2024)</span></div>
<div class="u5o-stat" role="listitem" style="background:#c2410c;"><b>$1.85 trillion</b><span>in damage (2024 dollars)</span></div>
<div class="u5o-stat" role="listitem" style="background:#1d4ed8;"><b>9,439</b><span>deaths</span></div>
</div>

<p style="text-align:center;font-size:.85em;opacity:.8;">Source: NOAA NCEI, U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters, 1980–2024. You'll explore this data in <a href="#u5o-text-2">Text 2</a>.</p>

**Think about it** before you start:

- Can you remember a **severe storm**? What did it feel like? Did you see any **damage**?
- What do you or your family do to **get ready** for a big storm? What problems do you face during one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💬 Ideas classmates often share (try your own first!)

- A **hurricane** brings heavy rain and extremely strong wind. A **blizzard** brings heavy snow and very strong wind.
- Both kinds of storms can cause a lot of **disruption**, **damage to property** and **harm to people**.
- Both can cause **extreme flooding**.
- Hurricanes and blizzards only happen during **certain months** of the year, and they tend to form and travel in **specific places** on Earth.
- "Storm damage" is a huge problem. To design solutions, we need to **break it into smaller problems**.
- A good solution should meet **criteria**, like reducing damage **without costing more than the damage itself**.

You'll test each of these ideas in the lessons ahead.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Saved details for Tell the Story. Kept in localStorage when it is available.
u5oDetails = {
  const KEY = "u5o-tell-the-story-v2";
  let state = {details: [], story: ""};
  try {
    const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY));
    if (saved && Array.isArray(saved.details)) state = {details: saved.details, story: typeof saved.story === "string" ? saved.story : ""};
  } catch (e) {}
  const subs = [];
  const persist = () => { try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(state)); } catch (e) {} };
  const notify = () => {
    persist();
    for (let i = subs.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
      const s = subs[i];
      if (s.el.isConnected) s.seen = true;
      else if (s.seen) { subs.splice(i, 1); continue; }
      s.fn();
    }
  };
  return {
    has: id => state.details.some(d => d.id === id),
    list: () => state.details.slice(),
    toggle: d => {
      state.details = state.details.some(x => x.id === d.id) ? state.details.filter(x => x.id !== d.id) : [...state.details, d];
      notify();
    },
    remove: id => { state.details = state.details.filter(x => x.id !== id); notify(); },
    story: () => state.story,
    setStory: t => { state.story = t; persist(); },
    clear: () => { state.details = []; state.story = ""; notify(); },
    subscribe: (el, fn) => subs.push({el, fn, seen: false})
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
    row.firstElementChild.textContent = it.detail;

}
```

As you watch, jot down the **main points**. Listen for:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔎 Where does "$170 billion" come from?

The **$170 billion** in the video's title is a **news estimate** for the winter storms of early 2026. It is **not** part of NOAA's billion-dollar disaster records in Texts 2 and 3, which end in **2024**. Different groups estimate storm costs in different ways, so their numbers don't always match. When you use a number as evidence, always ask: **who measured it, and how?**
:::

- Pick a **disaster type** (or all three).
- Switch between **how many** billion-dollar events happened each year and **how much** they cost.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔎 About these graphs

- **"Billion-dollar"** means the total damage from one event was **$1 billion or more**. Smaller storms are not counted, even if they caused a lot of harm.
- NOAA **adjusts for inflation**: a dollar in 1980 bought more than a dollar does today, so all costs are shown in **2024 dollars** to compare fairly.
- NOAA's full list has **403** billion-dollar disasters from 1980 to 2024. This page shows only the three types in your PTO. The rest are severe storms (like tornadoes and hail), droughts, wildfires and freezes.
- **Packet note:** in the PTO, the third graph's title repeats "Billion Dollar Hurricanes (Tropical Cyclones)," but its caption and data are for **flooding**. On this page it is labeled **Flooding**.
:::

## Text 3: Map of Billion-Dollar Storm Costs {#u5o-text-3}

Where in the US do these disasters cost the most? This map adds up the damage in each state from 1980 to 2024. **Darker colors = higher costs.** New York has a **thick outline**. Pick a disaster type, then tap or hover over a state.

```{ojs}
    fig.appendChild(map);
  } else {
    fig.appendChild(html`<p style="font-style:italic;">The map could not load right now. The table below has the same data.</p>`);
  }
  const ranked = u5oStates.slice().sort((a, b) => b[key] - a[key]);
  const top = ranked.slice(0, 10);
  const nyRank = ranked.findIndex(s => s.ab === "NY") + 1;
  const rows = top.map((s, i) => `<tr${s.ab === "NY" ? ' style="font-weight:800;"' : ""}><td style="padding:6px 8px;">${i + 1}</td><td style="padding:6px 8px;">${s.name}</td><td style="padding:6px 8px;">${fmt(s[key])}</td></tr>`).join("");
  const nyRow = nyRank > 10 ? `<tr style="font-weight:800;border-top:1px dashed currentColor;"><td style="padding:6px 8px;">${nyRank}</td><td style="padding:6px 8px;">New York</td><td style="padding:6px 8px;">${fmt(byName.get("New York")[key])}</td></tr>` : "";
  fig.appendChild(html`<div class="u5o-table-wrap"><table style="width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.92em;margin-top:8px;">
    <thead><tr style="border-bottom:2px solid currentColor;"><th style="padding:6px 8px;text-align:left;">Rank</th><th style="padding:6px 8px;text-align:left;">State or territory</th><th style="padding:6px 8px;text-align:left;">Cost, 1980–2024 (2024 dollars)</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>${rows}${nyRow}</tbody></table></div>`);
  fig.appendChild(html`<div style="font-size:.85em;opacity:.8;margin-top:6px;">Source: NOAA NCEI, U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters, state cost data, 1980–2024 (adjusted to 2024 dollars). Puerto Rico, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands are in the table but not on the map. State map: U.S. Census Bureau boundaries via us-atlas.</div>`);
  return fig;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

**One way to tell the story:**

1. Storms are a **huge and expensive problem** in the US. From 1980 to 2024 there were **136** billion-dollar winter storms, hurricanes and floods, costing about **$1.85 trillion** and causing **9,439 deaths**.
2. **Hurricanes** cause by far the most damage, but **floods** and **winter storms** cost billions too, and winter storms were still causing big losses in **2026**.
3. Billion-dollar storms are happening **more often** and costing **more**: 16 events in the 1980s, 37 in the 2010s and 34 in just 2020–2024.
4. The damage is worst along the **Gulf and Atlantic coasts**, but almost **every state** is affected. **New York** has had about **$79 billion** in damage, and the 2nd-highest winter storm costs in the country.
5. **Why it matters:** storm damage destroys homes, shuts down cities and costs lives. If we understand **how** storms cause damage (wind, rain and snow, flooding), we can **design solutions** to reduce it.

**Something to wonder about:** are costs rising only because storms are getting worse, or also because more people and buildings are in harm's way? Keep this question in mind as you look at the science of storms in this unit.
:::

# Brainstorming Initial Ideas {#u5o-brainstorm}

::: {.u5o-explain-box}
## 🛠️ Your task: design solutions to minimize storm damage

In this unit, your task is to **evaluate and design solutions to minimize storm damage** to people and property. To do that, you need to understand **how storms cause damage**. Storm damage is a **large set of connected problems**, so engineers **break it down into smaller problems** that they can solve one at a time.
:::

These engineering words come up all unit. They come from your PTO:

::: {.u5o-table-wrap}
| Word | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Problem** | The big challenge you want to solve | Storm damage in the US |
| **Subproblem** | A smaller piece of the big problem | Strong winds knock down power lines |
| **Criteria** | What a design **needs to do** to be successful (its requirements) | Keeps the power on during a storm |
| **Constraints** | **Limits** on the design, like materials, money or time | Must cost less than the city's budget |
| **Tradeoff** | Giving up one thing to get another | Burying power lines protects them from wind, but costs much more |
| **Design element** | A part of the solution: something you **change, add or take away** in the system | Adding a rain garden to soak up storm water |
:::

::: {.u5o-student-task}

There are no wrong answers yet. Use the tools below to organize your ideas, then copy them into your PTO.

```{ojs}
  const smallBtn = (label, aria, fn) => {
    const b = document.createElement("button");
    b.type = "button"; b.textContent = label; b.setAttribute("aria-label", aria);
    b.style.cssText = "min-width:44px;min-height:44px;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-weight:700;";
    b.onclick = fn;
    return b;
  };
  const paint = () => {
    opts.replaceChildren(...options.map(o => {
      const on = s.criteria.includes(o);
      return u5oChip(o, on, color, () => { s.criteria = on ? s.criteria.filter(x => x !== o) : [...s.criteria, o]; s.save(); paint(); });
    }));
    if (!s.criteria.length) {
      const li = document.createElement("li");
      li.style.cssText = "list-style:none;margin-left:-1.4em;font-size:.92em;color:#555;";
      li.textContent = "Nothing yet. Tap some criteria above.";
      list.replaceChildren(li);
      return;
    }
    list.replaceChildren(...s.criteria.map((c, i) => {
      const li = document.createElement("li");
      li.style.cssText = `margin:6px 0;${i < 3 ? "font-weight:800;" : ""}`;
      const row = document.createElement("div");
      row.style.cssText = "display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:6px;align-items:center;";
      const t = document.createElement("span");
      t.style.cssText = "flex:1 1 180px;";
      t.textContent = (i < 3 ? "⭐ " : "") + c;
      const swap = (a, b) => { const arr = s.criteria.slice(); [arr[a], arr[b]] = [arr[b], arr[a]]; s.criteria = arr; s.save(); paint(); };
      row.append(t,
        smallBtn("↑", "Move up: " + c, () => { if (i > 0) swap(i, i - 1); }),
        smallBtn("↓", "Move down: " + c, () => { if (i < s.criteria.length - 1) swap(i, i + 1); }));
      li.appendChild(row);
      return li;
    }));
  };
  ta.value = s.notes || "";
  ta.oninput = () => { s.notes = ta.value; s.save(); };
  wrap.querySelector(".u5o-copy").onclick = () => {
    const map = u5oCauses.map(c => {
      const items = [...s.picked.filter(p => p.startsWith(c.key + "|")).map(p => p.split("|")[1]), ...s.own.filter(o => o.cause === c.key).map(o => o.text)];
      return `${c.title}: ${items.join("; ") || "(none yet)"}`;
    }).join("\n");
    const crit = s.criteria.map((c, i) => `${i + 1}. ${c}${i < 3 ? " (top 3)" : ""}`).join("\n") || "(none yet)";
    u5oCopy(`Storm damage broken into smaller problems:\n${map}\n\nCriteria for a good solution:\n${crit}\n\nOther criteria or notes:\n${(s.notes || "").trim() || "(none)"}`, msg);
  };
  paint();
  return wrap;
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

**Breaking down storm damage.** One useful way is to sort by **what the storm does**:

- **Strong winds** knock down trees and power lines and damage buildings.
- **Heavy precipitation** (rain and snow) collapses roofs, closes roads and transit, and causes flash floods and landslides.
- **Flooding**, especially **coastal flooding**, fills homes, subways and tunnels with water.

Each of these leads to problems for **people**: power outages, injuries and deaths, lost work, and costly repairs. You'll study each subproblem in its own lesson: **Wind**, **Water** and **Flooding**.

**Criteria.** Strong answers include criteria that are:

- **Qualitative** (described in words): "protects people's lives," "is fair to every neighborhood."
- **Quantitative** (can be measured): "reduces damage **without costing more than the damage costs**," "keeps the power out for less than 24 hours."
- **Prioritized**: you can't always meet every criterion, so engineers decide which ones matter most. That choice is a **tradeoff**.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
u5oQuiz("u5o-brainstorm-quiz", "🛠️ Check Your Understanding: Engineering Ideas", [
  {
    q: "A city wants a flood wall. \"It must cost less than $50 million\" is an example of a…",
    options: ["Subproblem", "Constraint (a limit on the design)", "Design element", "Storm"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "A constraint is a limit on the design, like money, materials or time. A criterion is what the design needs to do, like \"keeps water out of the subway.\""
  },
  {
    q: "Why do engineers break \"storm damage\" into smaller problems?",
    options: ["Because big problems can't be studied", "Because each smaller problem (wind, rain and snow, flooding) has a different cause, so it needs a different solution", "Because it makes the problem disappear", "Because only one kind of storm causes damage"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Wind, precipitation and flooding happen in different ways. A solution works best when it targets the cause (mechanism) of one specific subproblem."
  },
  {
    q: "Burying power lines protects them from wind but costs much more than hanging them on poles. This is an example of a…",
    options: ["Tradeoff", "Myth", "Constraint that can never be met", "Subproblem"],
    correct: 0,
    explanation: "A tradeoff means giving up something (lower cost) to gain something else (protection from wind). Engineers decide if the benefit is worth the cost."
  }
])
```

## Revisiting the Performance Task {#u5o-revisiting}

At the end of each lesson, you'll return to your PTO to **evaluate a solution** for one subproblem. Each time, you'll practice a new **engineering component**.

::: {.u5o-table-wrap}
| After this lesson | Engineering component | Your PTO asks you to… |
|---|---|---|
| [Wind](unit5-wind.qmd) | **Identifying tradeoffs** | Explain how Winter Storm Jonas's strong winds formed and how the storm was carried across the country; list your top 3 criteria; evaluate the solution in the texts, its benefits and its costs. |
| [Water](unit5-water.qmd) | **Identifying constraints and limitations** | Explain how Jonas's heavy precipitation formed; evaluate a solution; name its criteria for success, its constraints, and its benefits and costs. |
| [Flooding](unit5-flooding.qmd) | **Design elements** | Explain what caused the flooding in Hurricane Sandy or in Marin County; design your own solution; describe its costs, benefits and constraints, and how each design element connects to the science. |
| [Unit Closing](unit5-closing.qmd) | **Final design** | Break "storm damage" into subparts and design a solution with **at least five design elements**, plus a written design rationale. |
:::

These are questions students often ask after Tell the Story, and where you'll investigate them:

::: {.u5o-table-wrap}
| Question | Where you'll investigate it |
|---|---|
| How do storms form and move? What causes high-speed winds? | [Wind](unit5-wind.qmd) |
| How does precipitation (rain and snow) form? Why do some storms drop so much? | [Water](unit5-water.qmd) |
| How can winter storms that drop snow also cause flooding? Why are some floods worse than others? | [Flooding](unit5-flooding.qmd) |
| Why are some disasters more costly than others? | Every lesson |
| How can costs and damage from storms be minimized? What would a good solution look like? | The Evaluate section of every lesson, then the [Unit Closing](unit5-closing.qmd) |
| Are the solutions the same for different kinds of storm disasters? | [Unit Closing](unit5-closing.qmd) |
:::
